analysis.one_liner: Would kill every federal regulation after three to seven years unless a new commission renews it.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single vote: after referral to two House committees and two subcommittees in January 1995, no hearings or floor action ever followed, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a nine-member Regulatory Sunset Commission, appointed by the President, with power to decide whether every federal regulation lives or dies. Existing rules would automatically expire after 7 years and new rules after 3, unless the Commission affirmatively authorized them to continue. The Commission's review criteria lean heavily toward cutting costs and burdens for regulated businesses, with only one criterion asking whether a rule protects public health and safety.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries would be the main winners. Under the bill, a rule an industry could not defeat through Congress or public comment would simply lapse on schedule unless a new commission chose to save it. Businesses, especially small businesses, would gain from criteria requiring the Commission to weigh compliance costs, effects on competition, and paperwork burdens [S3]. The stated public benefit is clearing out outdated and duplicative rules [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Every federal regulation would carry an expiration date — 7 years for existing rules, 3 years for new ones — forcing agencies to justify each rule to a new Regulatory Sunset Commission or lose it automatically [S3].

The Commission's 17 review criteria focus on whether rules are outdated, duplicative, impede competition, impose unnecessary economic burdens, or could rely on market mechanisms instead; businesses could testify and submit comments in every review [S3].
Information-collection requirements would have to be reduced where possible, with particular attention to small businesses [S3].

The bill's stated purpose is to make agencies regularly review their own rules and recommend terminating, keeping, or modifying them, which supporters presented as a way to clear obsolete and overlapping regulations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the risk. Workplace safety, food safety, environmental, consumer, and financial rules would all terminate by default unless a nine-member, unelected commission saved each one. The bill's criteria weigh cost to industry heavily and ask whether a rule protects public health and safety only once, and court challenges to a termination would be allowed only within 30 days [S3]. Agencies would also divert staff into perpetual review exercises, including designating a Regulatory Review Officer in every agency [S3].

drawbacks.text: Default termination puts every federal rule — from workplace and food safety to environmental and financial protections — at risk of expiring automatically unless a commission affirmatively renews it, flipping the burden from regulators to the public [S3].

Of the bill's 17 criteria for judging a rule, only one asks whether it is necessary to protect public health and safety, while a dozen focus on cost, burden, competition, and industry conditions [S3].
Judicial review would be sharply limited: a commission decision could be challenged in court only within 30 days of issuance, leaving little recourse if a protection was wrongly terminated [S3].

The bill would insert a new layer between Congress and agencies — a nine-member, unelected commission whose members are barred from other employment and removable by the President — to make binding decisions on rules that Congress itself wrote or delegated [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targets is real: regulations do pile up, and some become obsolete. But the design goes far past pruning. By making termination the default for every rule, weighting the criteria toward industry cost, and cutting court challenges to a 30-day window, the bill would put the entire federal protective apparatus on a treadmill where the loss of a safeguard happens automatically and saving it requires an affirmative act by a small appointed commission. The costs to the public outweigh the efficiency gains the bill promises.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in subcommittees of two House committees for the entire two-year Congress and died in January 1997, never reaching a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Chapman introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress, and it drew 7 cosponsors — 3 Republicans and 4 Democrats [S5][S4].
The House referred it to both the Government Reform and Oversight Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

Within three weeks it was sent down to the Subcommittee on National Economic Growth, Natural Resources and Regulatory Affairs and the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law — the last action ever recorded [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial protections are better off, because no rule ever faced automatic expiration. Federal agencies also kept their rulemaking authority intact rather than answering to a new sunset commission.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 3 Republicans and 4 Democrats among 7 cosponsors — but the bill never got a vote, so no one ever had to take a public position on it.

industries.industry: Regulated industries across the economy (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other regulated businesses)
industries.note: The bill would make expiration the default for every federal rule, so a regulation an industry could not defeat politically would lapse automatically unless a new commission saved it. Its review criteria weigh industry cost, competition effects, and paperwork heavily, while public health and safety appears once. The industry's gain comes directly at the expense of the protections ordinary people rely on.

The bill directs the commission to reduce information requirements, particularly for small businesses, which would cut compliance paperwork. The same automatic-expiration mechanism that relieves their burden would also strip protections their employees and customers depend on.

Every agency would have to review all of its rules on commission deadlines, publish responses in the Federal Register, and designate a Regulatory Review Officer reporting to the agency head. Keeping agencies' rulemaking authority intact serves the public here, since agency rules are the vehicle for the protections at stake.
